Gray wolves (Canis lupus) exhibit life-history traits finely tuned to their role as apex predators in temperate and boreal ecosystems. At a core body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], gestation lasts approximately 62 days [tg = approximately 62 days], a relatively brief period for a mammal of this size, reflecting the altricial state of the neonates. Newborn pups are entirely dependent on maternal care and weigh around 450 grams [Wwb = around 450 grams] at birth, a modest mass that belies their rapid growth trajectory during the subsequent weeks of intensive nursing. This small birth weight is thought to be constrained by the energetic costs of maintaining a large litter within a mobile hunting female. Field studies tracking tagged individuals indicate that pups first emerge from the den and begin consuming regurgitated solid food at roughly 47 days [tx = roughly 47 days], marking the weaning transition from exclusive milk ingestion to a mixed diet, by which point pups have grown to a wet weight at weaning of approximately 5250 grams [Wwx = approximately 5250 grams] at a temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. The relatively swift progression from neonatal dependence to the onset of weaning underscores the seasonal pressure wolves face to raise pups during a narrow window of prey abundance, a dynamic shaped by the harsh winters characteristic of their northern range.

Reproductive output in wolf populations is strongly density-dependent and modulated by prey availability. A dominant breeding female typically produces a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year], with average litter sizes averaging around 6 pups per litter [N_R_i = around 6 pups per litter]. This annual reproductive rate is relatively modest among large carnivores but is compensated by high pup survival under favorable conditions and extensive cooperative care from pack members. The success of each breeding attempt hinges on the pack's ability to defend a territory with sufficient ungulate biomass to support both the lactating female and the growing pups. Subordinate females within the pack rarely breed, a social suppression mechanism that concentrates reproductive effort in the dominant pair. Dispersal limitations and intense competition for breeding vacancies further regulate the effective population growth rate across the landscape. Longitudinal data from Yellowstone National Park demonstrate considerable interannual variation in litter size, linked to winter severity and subsequent calf-to-cow ratios in elk herds, illustrating how bottom-up trophic effects cascade through wolf life-history parameters.

Female wolves ultimately attain an adult body mass of approximately 40,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 40,000 grams], while males are considerably larger, reaching a mature weight of around 56,000 grams [Wwi = around 56,000 grams], among the most pronounced sexual size dimorphisms observed in canids. This dimorphism is believed to reflect divergent selective pressures: the larger body size in males confers advantages in territorial defense and competition for access to breeding females, whereas the smaller size of females may facilitate greater maneuverability during hunting and reduce the energetic demands of gestation and lactation. The ultimate wet weight values are consistent with measurements taken from adult specimens collected across the species' broad Holarctic distribution, with some geographic variation evident. Wolves inhabiting higher latitudes tend toward the upper end of this mass range, a pattern consistent with Bergmann's rule. Body size also influences pack dynamics, as larger males typically dominate feeding hierarchies at kills, though cooperative sharing ensures that all pack members meet their daily energetic requirements even during winter resource bottlenecks.

This delayed maturation, compared to smaller canids such as coyotes or foxes, is a consequence of the prolonged period required to attain adult body size and to acquire the social skills necessary for successful pack integration. Most individuals do not breed until they secure a dominant position within a pack or successfully establish a new territory with a mate, a process that often extends well beyond physiological puberty. Field observations of radio-collared wolves in Alaska and Scandinavia reveal that the age at first reproduction ranges from 22 to 36 months, depending on population density and the availability of vacant breeding territories. The energetic investment in growth and social learning during the pre-reproductive phase is substantial, with sub-adults gradually refining their hunting technique through repeated, often unsuccessful, attempts on large prey before reaching proficiency as breeding adults.

This value, recorded from a single exceptionally long-lived individual in a protected population, likely approaches the upper physiological limit of the species and is considerably higher than the typical lifespan of 6 to 8 years observed in most free-ranging populations. The discrepancy between maximum and average longevity highlights the immense selective pressure imposed by intraspecific aggression, starvation, and human-caused mortality. In captive settings, where wolves are shielded from these threats and receive consistent veterinary care, survival to ages beyond 15 years is not uncommon, reinforcing the notion that the species possesses a robust physiological capacity for extended life under ideal conditions. Lifespan is further modulated by body size, with larger individuals in some studies exhibiting slightly reduced longevity, a trade-off perhaps mediated by the higher cumulative energetic costs of supporting a large body mass across the years.
